title: How to Get Over a Breakup: A Week-by-Week Plan That Helps — cv.cm
description: How to get over a breakup: what is normal in the first weeks, a week-by-week plan, what helps, what makes it worse, how long it takes, and when to get help.
h1: How do you get over a breakup?
answer: Expect the first weeks to hurt: poor sleep, low appetite and replaying the relationship are normal. Stop contact and stop checking their social media, keep simple routines for sleep, food and movement, talk to friends, and write about what happened. Most people slowly feel better over weeks to months. If low mood lasts more than two weeks or you cannot cope, get professional help.

sections.h: What is normal in the first weeks
body: A breakup is a real loss. The NHS lists the end of a relationship alongside other losses that can cause grief. In Chinese this is called 失恋, in Japanese 失恋 too, in Korean 이별, and in Vietnamese thất tình. People everywhere describe the same things in the first weeks:

ul: Trouble falling asleep, or waking at 4 a.m. with your mind racing.
Losing your appetite, or eating much more than usual.
Replaying conversations and asking "what if" again and again.
Checking your phone for messages that do not come.
Waves of sadness, anger, relief, guilt and longing, sometimes in one hour.
Feeling that you do not know who you are without them.

body: None of this means something is wrong with you. It is what losing an important person feels like, even when the breakup was your choice.

sections.h: Why a breakup hurts so much
body: It is not only in your head. In one brain-imaging study (Kross and colleagues, 2011), people who had recently gone through an unwanted breakup looked at a photo of their ex while thinking about being rejected. Brain areas that also respond to physical pain became active. Social pain and physical pain overlap more than people expect.

A breakup also shakes your sense of self. Partners share friends, routines, plans and even parts of their identity. Researchers (Slotter, Gardner and Finkel, 2010) found that after a breakup people's self-concept became less clear, and that this loss of clarity predicted more emotional distress. That is why "who am I now?" is such a common feeling.

This also points to how recovery works. In another study (Larson and Sbarra, 2015), young adults who reflected on their breakup in a structured way over several weeks regained a clearer sense of who they were, and this went with less loneliness and fewer intrusive thoughts about the ex. Rebuilding "me" after "us" is the main work of getting over someone.
Everyone's timeline is different. Use this as a guide, not a test you pass or fail.

head: When
Main goal
What to do
rows: Week 1
Get through each day
Stop contact, mute their accounts, tell two friends, eat something three times a day, keep a fixed wake-up time
Weeks 2 to 4
Feel it without drowning in it
Cry when you need to, write for 15 minutes a day about what happened, walk or exercise most days, return their things
Month 2
Make sense of it
Write what you learned, what was yours and what was theirs; restart one hobby or plan that you dropped
Month 3 and after
Build your own life again
Try new things, meet new people, think about what you want in a partner next time

body: Bad days will come back, often on birthdays, holidays, or when you hear a certain song. A bad day after a good week is not going back to the start. It is part of the normal up-and-down of grief.

ul: No contact, or low contact if you share children or work. See cv.cm's article on the no contact rule for how to do it.
Sleep at regular times. Put your phone outside the bedroom at night if you check it.
Move your body. The NHS suggests regular exercise to help mood and sleep. A daily walk counts.
Eat regular meals, even small ones.
Talk to people. Friends, family, a counsellor, or a support group. Say what you need: "I don't need advice, I just need to talk."
Write. Write what happened, what you miss, what you do not miss, and what you want next. Writing gives the replaying mind somewhere to go.
Do one thing that is only yours: a class, a sport, a trip, a project you put off during the relationship.
Make a short list of the real problems in the relationship. Read it when you start to remember only the good parts.

body: You do not have to do all of this. Pick two or three and repeat them.

Try instead
rows: Checking their social media
In one study, checking an ex's profile went with more distress, more longing and less personal growth
Mute or unfollow so you do not have to decide each time
Rereading old chats and photos
Restarts the longing every time
Move them to one folder you do not open for now
Asking friends for news about them
Keeps you living in their life, not yours
Ask friends to not tell you unless you ask
Drinking or using drugs to numb it
The NHS warns these can make mental health worse
Call a friend, go outside, or write
A rebound just to stop the pain
You carry the hurt into the new relationship
Date when you are curious about new people, not escaping
Staying in bed and cancelling everything
Isolation deepens low mood
Keep one small plan every day, even a short walk
Blaming yourself for everything
It is rarely true and slows healing
Write down your part and their part, separately

sections.h: How long it takes, and how you know you are moving on
body: There is no fixed rule. A few weeks for a short relationship, many months for a long one or a marriage, are both normal. Popular formulas, such as "half the length of the relationship", have no research behind them.

ul: You go hours, then days, without thinking of them.
You can think of them with less heat: some sadness, but not a rush of hope or anger.
You stopped checking whether they are online or who they follow.
You can see what did not work, not only what you lost.
You are making plans that have nothing to do with them.

body: If you still hope to get back together, read cv.cm's decision guide on whether to get back together before acting on it. And if you want to understand your own patterns in relationships, cv.cm's attachment style test is a good place to start.

Sadness after a breakup is normal. But grief can turn into depression or anxiety that does not lift on its own. The NHS suggests seeing a doctor if you have had low mood for more than two weeks, if you are struggling to cope, or if your own efforts are not helping. A counsellor or therapist can also help if the breakup brought up older pain.
Get help sooner if you cannot work or study for weeks, stop eating, cannot sleep for many nights, or use alcohol to get through each day.

body.note: If you have thoughts of hurting yourself or ending your life, please contact a crisis line or emergency services where you live now. You do not have to wait until it gets worse. If the relationship was abusive or your ex is threatening you, a domestic violence helpline, such as loveisrespect.org or thehotline.org in the US, or a local service where you live, can help.

faq.q: How long does it take to get over a breakup?
faq.a: It varies from a few weeks to many months, depending on how long and how close the relationship was, how it ended, and how much support you have. There is no correct timeline.

faq.q: Why can't I stop thinking about my ex?
faq.a: Replaying the relationship is the mind trying to make sense of a loss. Contact, checking their profile and rereading chats keep feeding it, so cutting those down usually makes the thoughts less frequent over time.

faq.q: Is it normal to still love my ex?
faq.a: Yes. Love does not switch off when a relationship ends. You can still care about someone and know the relationship was not right.

faq.q: Should I stay friends with my ex?
faq.a: Not right away. Friendship is easier after a period of no contact, once neither of you is hoping for more. Some people never become friends with an ex, and that is fine.

faq.q: How do I get over someone I still see every day?
faq.a: Keep contact polite and practical, avoid private chats, and limit time in shared spaces where you can. Build more of your day around other people and activities so they take up less of it.
Not always, but dating mainly to stop the pain often carries old hurt into something new. It is better to wait until you feel curious about new people rather than desperate to stop feeling sad.
